clue.text: Chap not returning after dance

indicators.note: after places the reversed piece behind the man's name in the answer

parts.note: Charles is a man's name, so a chap

indicators.note: returning means the word not is read from its end back to its start

parts.note: taken as written before it is turned

explanation.surface: A man who left a dance hall and never came back.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively 1920s jazz-age step named after a city in South Carolina.

clue.text: Conservative remains ready

parts.note: ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A Tory's ashes are prepared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' is a noun here: 'the ready' is British slang for cash in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready money, or the ready, is money available for immediate spending.

clue.text: A maiden's holding century up for unidentified cricketer

indicators.note: holding means the first letter and the word for the maiden wrap round the reversed piece

parts.note: taken as written
a maiden is a girl, she or her

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word for a century reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a ton is a hundred, or a century

explanation.surface: A bowler's maiden over keeps a hundred runs from being scored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maiden' and 'century' look like cricket terms but give HER and TON. A N OTHER is the placeholder name in British team lists for a player yet to be named.
explanation.definitionFit: A. N. Other is the stock name in a British team sheet for a player not yet chosen.

clue.text: Get angry, having to get rid of a college? That's not hard

parts.note: to get rid of is to lose

indicators.note: H is hard in pencil grading, so not hard means that letter is dropped from the phrase for a college

parts.note: a college is one school

explanation.surface: Someone furious at having to shut a college, though it is easy enough.
explanation.walkthrough: LOSE ONE SCHOOL minus H gives the phrase. 'That's not hard' sounds like a comment on difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's temper or composure, to stop being calm.

clue.text: Our team picked up match official's anger for certain

indicators.note: picked up in a down clue means the word for our team is read upwards

parts.note: our team is us
a referee, or ref, officiates a match
ire is anger

explanation.surface: Our side noticed the referee getting angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' turns US into SU; it is not a homophone signal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Surefire means guaranteed to succeed, dependable.

clue.text: Admitting doctor has to avoid being swamped

indicators.note: has to avoid means the word for drowning loses the doctor's abbreviation

parts.note: drowning is being swamped by water

explanation.surface: A medic confesses he must stay out of flood water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitting' looks like a hospital admission, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Owning, as in owning up, means confessing or acknowledging.

clue.text: Theatre mainly for men

indicators.note: mainly asks for most of the word for theatre, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: the stage is the theatre as a profession

explanation.surface: A men-only theatre, perhaps a club staging shows for gentlemen.
explanation.walkthrough: A STAG party or night is one for men only, so the adjectival use fits 'for men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stag describes an all-male gathering, such as a party held before a wedding for the groom.

clue.text: Chap going round ancient city is example of this?

definitions.text: Chap going round ancient city is example of this?

indicators.note: going round means the man's name encloses the following letters

parts.note: Tom is a man's name
Ur is the ancient city of Mesopotamia
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man visiting an ancient city is engaged in sightseeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' puts UR IS inside TOM; the whole clue then describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sightseeing at historic places is a central part of holiday travel.

clue.text: What Labour not laughing represents, seeing Tory in trouble

definitions.note: labour is giving birth, so this is giving and no laughing matter

indicators.note: in trouble means the letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim-faced Labour Party watching a Tory in difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' signals an anagram of SEEING TORY. The definition is cryptic: labour is giving (birth), and giving is open-handedness.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-handed giving is the core of liberality, and labour is giving birth.

clue.text: Take several horses to farrier, having limited budget

definitions.meaning: to shoe a string, a string being a group of horses kept by one stable
a very small sum of money to work with

explanation.surface: A stable owner on a tight budget takes the horses to be shod.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer as SHOE (what the farrier does) and STRING (a stable's horses); 'having' just links the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on a meagre allowance is doing it on this, an idiom for scant funds.

clue.text: Brooke, so to speak, a poet coming to premature end

definitions.note: said out loud, the poet's name Brooke is brook, a small stream

indicators.note: coming to a premature end means the poet's name is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: Robert Burns, the Scottish poet

explanation.surface: Rupert Brooke, a poet who died young, is described.
explanation.walkthrough: Brooke and Burns both look like poets here; Rupert Brooke died at 27, which makes the surface apt. A burn is the Scottish word for a stream.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland and northern England a small stream or brook is called by this word.

clue.text: Easy victory for Arab competitor?

definitions.meaning: a contest that one side wins without any real opposition
an Arab is a breed of horse, so a contest for it is a race for one horse

explanation.surface: An Arab horse wins a race at a canter.
explanation.definitionFit: A contest with only one realistic contender is so described, from horse racing.

clue.text: Mum's rings get lost!

parts.note: mum means silent, and 'sh' is the call for silence
two rings look like two letter Os

explanation.surface: Mother's rings have gone missing, an exclamation of dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' is not mother but 'quiet', as in 'mum's the word'.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation used to send someone or something away, like 'go away!'

clue.text: Bread producer — cafe and inn I supply, right?

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, so the words are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A baker offering to stock a cafe and an inn with loaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a verb but is the adverb 'supply' (supplely), the anagram signal for CAFE INN I, with R added. 'Bread' is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, and a financier provides capital, so produces the cash.

clue.text: Twenty enter — it represents a record for the game

definitions.text: it represents a record for the game

parts.note: a score is twenty
to board a train or ship is to enter it

explanation.surface: Twenty people go in to set a record for a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twenty' and 'enter' are both read as words of the surface; they give SCORE and BOARD.
explanation.definitionFit: The display at a sports ground shows the running tally of a match.

clue.text: Transport accommodating English and French going over?

definitions.text: Transport accommodating English and French going over?

indicators.note: accommodating means the verb for transport holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: to transport is to carry

indicators.note: going over means the letters for English and French are turned around

explanation.surface: A vessel that carries English and French travellers across the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going over' turns E FR into RFE, which 'accommodating' puts inside CARRY after CA. The whole clue also describes a cross-Channel boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel that conveys vehicles and passengers across water, as between England and France.

clue.text: Fake American detective

parts.note: a fake is a sham
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A phoney private eye from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: Shamus is American slang for a private investigator.
explanation.definitionFit: US slang for a private investigator or police officer.

clue.text: Fighter expected to add 50 to tally

parts.note: due means expected, as a train due at noon
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
a tally is a list or count

explanation.surface: A boxer due to add fifty to their record.
explanation.walkthrough: DUE, then L, then LIST; 'to add' merely links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fights a formal duel, a combatant in single combat.

clue.text: Aged widow going again round entrance to churchyard

indicators.note: round means the word for going again wraps around another letter

parts.note: a fire relit is going again

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An elderly widow walking round the churchyard gate once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going again' is a fire RELIT, not a person walking; C goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Relict is an old word for a woman who has survived her husband, often in legal or epitaph use.

clue.text: Supply the flower to be taken round

indicators.note: to be taken round means the flower's name wraps around the word the

parts.note: the lily is a flower
taken as written

explanation.surface: Provide the flower to be carried about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is not the verb but the adverb from supple, nimbly.
explanation.definitionFit: Supply as the adverb of supple means in a flexible, graceful way.

clue.text: Completely wrong? Not so

parts.note: out means wrong, as in a guess that is way out
not so wrong, that is, correct

explanation.surface: Someone asks if they are utterly mistaken and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so' answers the question 'wrong?', giving its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Outright means wholly or entirely, as in winning without dispute.

clue.text: Offered to hold outrageous dance

indicators.note: to hold means the word for offered goes around the next piece

parts.note: gave means offered
OTT stands for over the top, so outrageous

explanation.surface: Someone offered to hold a wild dance.
explanation.walkthrough: OTT (over the top) is British shorthand for excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A gavotte is an old French court dance in moderate duple time.

clue.text: Religion very full of suggestion

indicators.note: full of means the word for very contains the next piece

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
a hint is a suggestion

explanation.surface: A faith that is highly suggestive.
explanation.definitionFit: Shinto is the native faith of Japan, based on reverence for kami spirits.

clue.text: Union compact with Labour backing — the rot, unhappily, set in

indicators.note: set in means the rearranged letters go inside the reversed abbreviation
backing means the abbreviation for Labour is reversed

parts.note: Lab is short for the Labour Party

indicators.note: unhappily signals that the words the rot are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A political pact with Labour support, but decay has crept in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns LAB into BAL; 'unhappily' turns THE ROT into ETROTH; 'set in' places that inside BAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An engagement is a promise or agreement to marry, a pact leading to union.

clue.text: English service not a highly regarded thing?

indicators.note: not means the letter a is taken out of the word for the service

parts.note: the navy is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: An English service judged not to be one of the best.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on 'the envy of', said of something others admire and covet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is the object of others' envy is admired and coveted, hence highly regarded.

clue.text: Long journey ends in disillusionment for the monk

indicators.note: ends in means the final letters of each of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: A monk's long pilgrimage ends in disappointment.
explanation.definitionFit: A trek is an arduous journey, especially on foot.

clue.text: Affirm extreme dislike? Not half

indicators.note: not half means only one half of the word for dislike is kept, its front portion

parts.note: an aversion is a strong dislike

explanation.surface: Someone confirms they hate something, then says 'not half!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' looks like the British exclamation meaning 'very much', but here it cuts AVERSION to its first four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to state or assert something firmly.

clue.text: A talk about man — it's explosive stuff, in theory

indicators.note: about means the word for talk goes around the man's name

parts.note: natter is chatty talk
Tim is a man's name

explanation.surface: A chat about a man who turns out to be dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps NATTER around TIM after its N. Matter meeting antimatter would annihilate, so it is explosive in theory.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimatter is made of antiparticles; meeting ordinary matter, it releases huge energy, a largely theoretical substance.

clue.text: Period of bewilderment for listeners

definitions.note: a span of time, as in 'in those days'

indicators.note: for listeners means the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: a daze is a state of bewilderment

explanation.surface: A spell of confusion experienced by an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: A plural run of time, as in 'one's schooldays', denotes an era or span.

clue.text: Confidence and assurance needed to make jam

parts.note: bottle is British slang for nerve or courage
neck is British slang for cheek or brazen self-assurance

explanation.surface: Nerve and self-belief are needed to make preserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jam' is a traffic jam, not a preserve. BOTTLE and NECK are both British slang: courage and cheek.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow point where traffic or flow is held up, causing congestion.
